claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi', and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
Debugging AWS CDK was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi deployments are faster due to direct execution.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility, while AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, the SST team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployment.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments enables more advanced deployment workflows, at the docs URL /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at /resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (not in Pulumi Cloud).
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
The SST team has said, repeatedly since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs 'What is SST' page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published package.json for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The `sst/sst` repository is now hosted as `anomalyco/sst`, and its platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST deploys, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations, and Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.

Nitric states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," and its official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.

Defang's Pulumi provider is described in its repository as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result; Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
SST does not require a Pulumi account to work, and SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket rather than Pulumi's hosted service.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly with Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (more stars) than SST itself.
The team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails enforceable centrally, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.
SST users are running Pulumi's engine whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
The blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
The docs page /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ exists and describes Pulumi engine mechanics.
The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ is titled 'Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi'.
